record.original_question: For materials undergoing phase transformations with fine microstructure, explain why fine microstructure forms, predict its morphology, and determine the material properties at macroscopic scales much larger than the microstructure scale, ideally within a suitably formulated dynamical theory that accounts for interface kinetics.

evidence.quote: Why does fine microstructure form? To what extent can we predict its morphology? What are the properties of the material at a macroscale much larger than the microscale of the microstructure?
it is neither clear what such a theory should be

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a continuum model of an elastic solid occupying a reference domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^3$, whose deformations $y:\Omega\times[0,T]\to\mathbb{R}^3$ are governed by a stored-energy functional
$$ E[y] = \int_\Omega W(\nabla y(x),\theta(x))\,dx, $$
where $\theta$ is temperature and $W:\mathbb{R}^{3\times 3}_+\times\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is a frame-indifferent multi-well energy density whose set of energy-minimizing gradients $K(\theta)=\{F:W(F,\theta)=\min W(\cdot,\theta)\}$ corresponds to distinct martensitic variants (so that $W$ is, in general, non-quasiconvex). Material points may also satisfy a dynamical evolution law of the form
$$ \rho\, y_{tt} = \mathrm{Div}\, T(\nabla y, \nabla y_t,\theta) + f, $$
augmented by a kinetic relation governing the motion and nucleation of phase interfaces.

For such a material undergoing phase transformations that exhibit fine microstructure (rapidly oscillating gradient fields taking values close to $K(\theta)$):

(a) Provide a rigorous mathematical explanation, within a suitably formulated dynamical theory incorporating interface kinetics, of why fine microstructure forms, rather than merely characterizing it as a non-attainment phenomenon for the static energy functional.

(b) Predict the resulting morphology of the microstructure (length scales, geometric patterns of the laminates or more complex arrangements, and their dependence on boundary conditions, loading history, and kinetics).

(c) Determine the effective macroscopic material response on scales much larger than the microstructural length scale: in particular, identify a well-posed homogenized/relaxed dynamical theory whose solutions describe the observed average behavior of materials with such microstructure.
artifact.status_search_result: The question is a long-standing open program in the mathematical theory of martensitic phase transformations and nonlinear elasticity. While partial results exist (quasiconvex envelopes, Young measure characterizations of laminates, rigidity results, and special dynamical models with interface kinetics), no general dynamical theory predicting microstructure formation and macroscopic effective behavior is known. It is presented as an open problem in recent surveys.

status_evidence.title: Some open problems in elasticity (zbMATH)
status_evidence.snippet: Lists microstructure formation, prediction, and macroscale behavior among open problems in elasticity.
status_evidence.claim: The problem is posed as currently open.
